newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia employers push for cuts in work benefits.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia employers push for cuts in work benefits.

text.p: The Slovenian Association of Employers said on Monday the general collective agreement between employers and unions should be changed from the start of 1997.
The association said the pact, introduced in 1990 and renewed in 1993, should be amended so bonuses paid to employees would be reduced in financially troubled industrial sectors.
"The change is necessary because workforce expenses are seriously diminishing the competitiveness of Slovenian companies," the association's secretary Vitko Ros told Reuters.
He said employers were pushing for cuts in sick benefits, compensation strike pay, redundancy pay, holiday benefits and daily allowances in troubled industrial sectors.
"Most companies in labour-intensive sectors and a lot of exporters claim they could face bankruptcy if workforce costs are not reduced," Ros said.
The average gross monthly salary in Slovenia was 131,803 tolars ($970) in July and rose 14 percent in the first seven months of 1996 compared to the same period of 1995.
According to the current agreement, the average holiday pay is the same as an average monthly salary, while the average monthly sick pay represents 80 percent of a full salary.
Slovenian unions threatened they would organise a general strike if employers stood by their decision.
"We are not ready to negotiate about workers' rights which are already minimal," said Rajko Lesjak, secretary of the Free Unions of Slovenia, the country's largest union association.
The government has already been forced to make concessions to workers following a number of public sector strikes this year.
Slovenia is due to hold its third general election on November 10.
